IDEA: Third-base coach send/hold decisions; owner is the third-base coach with an advance and analytics staff; the decision comes up in nearly every game whenever a runner could try for home on a single or fly ball; league-wide historical cases number in the thousands per season through public play-by-play and tracking feeds; the observable outcome is safe, out, or held and the scoring that followed; the simple baseline is the coach's judgment plus a fixed rule like "send with two outs"; the intervention is a pregame card estimating break-even send probability by out, score, inning, runner sprint speed, fielder arm strength and fielder distance.
ASSUMPTION: Public tracking data records fielder throw distance, arm strength and runner position at the moment of the send decision accurately enough to rebuild the counterfactual for held runners.
ASSUMPTION: Held runners are a selected sample, so retrospective tests will be biased unless they model what would have happened on holds.
ASSUMPTION: Criterion (c) may fail if sends with a real edge are rare per club-season and most decisions are already obvious.
UNKNOWN: club_send_hold_baseline_policy
UNKNOWN: public_tracking_coverage_for_held_runners

IDEA: Starting pitcher removal timing; owner is the manager and pitching coach; the decision comes up every game, with several candidate moments per start; league-wide cases number in the thousands of starts per season, each with many decision points, in public pitch-by-pitch data; the observable outcome is run expectancy change after the pull or stay, plus later reliever workload; the simple baseline is a pitch-count or times-through-order rule; the intervention is a live estimate of the starter's current effectiveness from velocity, release and command drift compared with the specific available reliever.
ASSUMPTION: Within-game velocity and command decline predicts near-term run prevention beyond what times-through-order already captures.
ASSUMPTION: Counterfactual outcomes for the pitcher not used cannot be observed, so the evaluation relies on modeled rather than observed outcomes; this weakens (b).
ASSUMPTION: Workload carryover to later games, and the resulting injury risk, may outweigh single-game gains and is poorly observable in public data.
UNKNOWN: club_current_pull_rule
UNKNOWN: reliever_availability_ground_truth_for_own_club

IDEA: Stolen base and pickoff attempt choices under the pitch-clock disengagement limits; owners are the first-base coach, the manager and the runner; the decision comes up many times per game; league-wide cases number in the thousands of attempts and far more non-attempts per season in public data; the observable outcome is success, caught, pickoff or balk, plus the base-out state; the simple baseline is a green light for runners above a sprint-speed threshold; the intervention is a per-matchup estimate combining pitcher time to plate, catcher pop time, disengagements remaining, count and lead distance.
ASSUMPTION: Lead distance and jump data are publicly available at enough resolution to model non-attempts, not just attempts.
ASSUMPTION: League-wide adaptation since the rule change may have already removed most of the edge, which threatens (c).
UNKNOWN: public_lead_distance_data_availability
UNKNOWN: club_baserunning_green_light_policy

IDEA: Daily lineup rest-day selection for position players; owner is the manager with the performance staff; the decision comes up daily across a 162-game season; league-wide cases number in the thousands of player-days rested or played per season through public lineup cards; the observable outcome is next-game and next-week batted-ball quality, sprint speed trends, and later injured-list placements; the simple baseline is a fixed rest cadence or day-game-after-night-game rule; the intervention is a fatigue signal from public sprint speed, bat speed and exit velocity trends that suggests which days to rest.
ASSUMPTION: Public bat-speed and sprint-speed drift reflects fatigue rather than noise, swing changes or undisclosed minor injuries.
ASSUMPTION: Without private workload and medical data, (d) may fail because the club already holds much better information than the public signal.
ASSUMPTION: The value per correctly timed rest day may be too small to reach (c) unless it prevents injured-list stints.
UNKNOWN: link_between_public_fatigue_signal_and_injury
UNKNOWN: club_internal_rest_protocol

IDEA: Promotions between minor-league levels; owner is the farm director; the decision comes up continuously across the season; league-wide cases number in the hundreds to thousands of promotions per season through public MiLB transactions; the observable outcome is performance at the new level and time to the next promotion or demotion; the simple baseline is promoting on surface stats or age-for-level; the intervention ranks promotion readiness using public Statcast-style minor-league tracking (where it exists), plate discipline and contact quality rather than surface outcomes.
ASSUMPTION: Promotion outcomes are confounded because only players already judged ready get promoted, so a retrospective test needs a quasi-experimental design.
ASSUMPTION: Public minor-league tracking coverage differs by level and year, which may break (d) at the lower levels.
ASSUMPTION: The value of better promotion timing may only show up years later, which delays observing (b).
UNKNOWN: public_milb_tracking_coverage_by_level_year
UNKNOWN: club_promotion_criteria

IDEA: Waiver claims on designated-for-assignment players; owner is the front office; the decision comes up weekly or more often during the season; league-wide cases number in the hundreds of DFAs per season in public transaction logs; the observable outcome is whether claimed players produce value or are quickly DFA'd again; the simple baseline is claiming based on prior MLB results and options remaining; the intervention flags DFA'd players whose underlying pitch quality or contact metrics far exceed their surface results.
ASSUMPTION: Waiver priority and counterparty claims limit which players a club can actually acquire, which weakens control over the outcome.
ASSUMPTION: This overlaps the minor-league free agent triage family, which tied a prior-MLB-time rule, so the edge may again be small.
UNKNOWN: claim_success_rate_given_waiver_priority
UNKNOWN: differentiation_from_R001_result

IDEA: Bullpen warm-up decisions, including relievers who warm but do not enter; owner is the manager and bullpen coach; the decision comes up most games; league-wide historical cases are poorly recorded in public data; the outcome is reliever effectiveness and availability on following days; the simple baseline is warming on fixed triggers like a baserunner in a late close game; the intervention estimates the cost of a warm-up against the likelihood the reliever will be needed.
ASSUMPTION: Criterion (b) likely fails because public data rarely records warm-ups that do not lead to an appearance.
ASSUMPTION: This could only be tested on the club's own private logs, which limits league-wide statistical power under (a).
UNKNOWN: public_warmup_records_existence

IDEA: Catcher assignment for each starting pitcher; owner is the manager; the decision comes up daily; league-wide cases number in the thousands of pitcher-catcher pairings per season through public lineups and pitch data; the observable outcome is called-strike rate, pitch results and runs allowed for each pairing; the simple baseline is a fixed personal-catcher arrangement or the regular starter catching; the intervention estimates pairing-specific effects on called strikes and pitch-mix execution.
ASSUMPTION: Pairing effects are distinct and stable beyond each catcher's individual framing skill; this may not hold.
ASSUMPTION: The automated ball-strike challenge system could shrink framing value, which threatens (c) going forward.
UNKNOWN: pairing_effect_stability
UNKNOWN: abs_impact_on_framing_value

IDEA: Intentional walk, infield-in and bunt choices in close late-game situations; owner is the manager; the decision comes up a few times per week; league-wide cases number in the thousands per season in public play-by-play; the observable outcome is the change in win expectancy; the simple baseline is a generic win-expectancy chart; the intervention adjusts for the specific batter, on-deck hitter, pitcher and fielder ranges.
ASSUMPTION: Criterion (c) may fail because these decisions are already well studied and the gains left at the margin are small.
ASSUMPTION: Treating many small decisions as summing to a meaningful season value assumes they are independent and the effects do not cancel; this is unverified.
UNKNOWN: residual_edge_over_public_win_expectancy_tables

ASSUMPTION: Across all families, a high number of league-wide cases does not guarantee power if the true edge per decision is tiny compared with game-outcome noise.
ASSUMPTION: The club may already run equivalent tools, so the real baseline may be stronger than any simple rule assumed here.
UNKNOWN: cubs_existing_tooling_for_in_game_decisions
UNKNOWN: supplied_evidence

text:
IDEA: Third-base coach send/hold decisions. Owner: third-base coach, with input from the advance and analytics staff. Decision: send or hold a runner on singles and doubles with a play at the plate possible, several times per series. Cases: every club generates these each season, and public tracking data covers multiple seasons, so league-wide cases are numerous. Outcome: safe, out, or held, and the resulting run expectancy, all publicly observable. Baseline: the coach's judgment, or a rule keyed only to runner sprint speed. Intervention: a pre-pitch card combining runner sprint speed, each outfielder's public arm strength and transfer time, outs, inning, score and on-deck hitter quality, giving a break-even send probability per situation.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (a) partly, because only sends produce an observed safe/out outcome; holds are censored, so tests of the counterfactual send depend on modeled throw outcomes.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (c) possibly, because aggregate run value per club-season may be small unless current coaching is systematically too conservative or too aggressive.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (d) possibly, because clubs may already give coaches arm-strength cards; public data may not show what the coach actually used.
UNKNOWN: league_wide_send_hold_case_count_per_season
UNKNOWN: whether_public_tracking_records_held_runner_opportunities_consistently

IDEA: Starting pitcher removal timing within a game. Owner: manager and pitching coach. Decision: remove or continue the starter at each batter boundary from the middle innings onward, every start. Cases: every start league-wide over many seasons, so the number of decision points is far larger than the number of starts. Outcome: the plate-appearance outcomes that follow, publicly observable. Baseline: a pitch-count threshold or times-through-order rule. Intervention: a per-batter estimate of starter-versus-reliever expected run value using within-game velocity and spin decay, upcoming hitter handedness and quality, and the reliever availability already known to the club.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (a) in the causal sense, because pitchers left in are selected for looking good, so naive retrospective comparisons are confounded.
ASSUMPTION: Overlaps with the explored bullpen-availability family; it is distinct only if the focus is on the starter's in-game decay signal rather than the bullpen's state.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (c) partly, because the long-run cost of starter workload, such as injury, is not observed within the game, so short-run run value may overstate the gain.
UNKNOWN: magnitude_of_within_game_velocity_decay_signal_beyond_pitch_count

IDEA: Infield-in versus infield-back with a runner on third and fewer than two outs. Owner: manager and infield coach. Decision: infield depth on each qualifying plate appearance, many times per season. Cases: the base-out state recurs throughout every season for all clubs, and public tracking includes fielder positioning, so cases are numerous. Outcome: whether the run scored, hit or out, and the batted-ball result, all public. Baseline: infield in late and close, back otherwise. Intervention: a batter- and pitcher-specific ground-ball and exit-velocity model plus runner speed, giving the break-even inning and score for each matchup.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (c) possibly, because the situation is frequent but the per-decision value difference may be small.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (a) partly, because public positioning data may not distinguish deliberate infield-in from shading, and the 2023 shift restrictions changed the feasible alignments, which shortens the comparable history.
UNKNOWN: whether_public_positioning_data_labels_infield_in_reliably_across_seasons

IDEA: Minor-league level-promotion timing. Owner: player development director and farm director. Decision: promote, hold or demote a player between minor-league levels, evaluated continually and acted on many times per season. Cases: all 30 organizations move many players between levels each season, and public minor-league transaction and stat records exist, so cases are numerous. Outcome: performance and strikeout/walk changes at the new level, and eventual MLB arrival, publicly observable with lags. Baseline: promote after a fixed time at a level or when surface stats such as OPS or ERA cross a threshold. Intervention: a model favoring stable, fast-stabilizing indicators (contact rate, chase rate, minor-league tracking where public, strikeout-minus-walk rate) and age-relative-to-level, estimating the probability of success at the next level.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (a) causally, because promotion decisions are selected on private information, so retrospective tests compare promoted players to held ones who differ in unobserved ways.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (b) partly, because the long-run development outcome is delayed by years and confounded by injuries and later coaching.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (d) possibly, because minor-league tracking data are less public than MLB data and access may be restricted.
UNKNOWN: public_availability_of_minor_league_tracking_metrics_by_level_and_season
UNKNOWN: whether_too_early_promotion_has_measurable_developmental_harm

IDEA: Minor-league pitcher workload and progression limits. Owner: player development and the medical/performance staff. Decision: innings, pitch-count and rest limits for each developing pitcher, set every outing. Cases: a large number of outings each season across all organizations. Outcome: public injured-list placements, velocity changes and missed time, observable with noise. Baseline: a uniform innings-increase cap year over year or fixed pitch counts by level. Intervention: an individualized limit using public velocity trends within and across outings, age and workload history, flagging pitchers whose decline pattern resembles past injured comparables.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (b) badly, because minor-league injury reporting is incomplete and clubs may disguise injuries as roster moves.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (a) for causal tests, because workload choices respond to private medical information.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (c) uncertainly, because the payoff depends on rare high-cost injuries, which gives low statistical power even with many outings.
UNKNOWN: completeness_of_public_minor_league_injured_list_data

IDEA: Late-game defensive substitution. Owner: manager and bench coach. Decision: replace a weaker defender with a stronger one when leading late, many games per season. Cases: every club makes this choice, or passes on it, routinely, so league-wide cases are numerous. Outcome: subsequent defensive plays, the lost bat if the game is tied or extended, and the result, all publicly observable. Baseline: substitute when leading by a small margin in the final innings. Intervention: a per-situation estimate trading expected defensive runs saved over the remaining outs against the expected offensive loss if the substitute's spot comes up again, including extra-innings probability.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (c) possibly, because the remaining outs are few, so value per decision is small and only adds up if the baseline is badly miscalibrated.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (a) partly, because the substitute's defensive impact over a few outs is mostly unobservable noise; tests must rely on modeled defensive value.
UNKNOWN: whether_current_league_practice_differs_measurably_from_model_break_even

IDEA: Manager replay challenges on non-ball-strike plays. Owner: replay coordinator and manager. Decision: challenge or not on close plays at the bases, tag plays and catches, multiple opportunities per game. Cases: challenges occur league-wide many times per season and outcomes are published, so cases are numerous. Outcome: overturned, confirmed or stands, publicly reported. Baseline: challenge whenever the video room's confidence crosses a gut threshold, with conservative behavior early in games. Intervention: a break-even model combining overturn probability, the play's run or win-expectancy swing, the inning and the option value of retaining the challenge.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (d) partly, because the key input, the video room's own read, is private, and public data show only challenged plays, not unchallenged close plays.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (c) possibly, because overturn value is concentrated in a small number of high-leverage plays per club-season.
ASSUMPTION: Overlaps conceptually with the explored ABS challenge-strategy family; it is distinct only because the inputs are video confidence and play leverage rather than pitch location.
UNKNOWN: availability_of_unchallenged_close_play_records

IDEA: Intentional walk decisions after the automatic intentional walk rule. Owner: manager. Decision: issue an intentional walk in base-out and score states where it is possible, several times per month. Cases: league-wide intentional walks and comparable non-walk situations recur each season, so cases are numerous. Outcome: subsequent plate appearances and runs, publicly observable. Baseline: walk the dangerous hitter with first base open late in close games. Intervention: a matchup-specific run- and win-expectancy comparison using the batter and on-deck hitter's pitch-type vulnerabilities against the current pitcher, and the platoon and bench state.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (c) likely, because intentional walks are less frequent in modern play, so total value per club may be small.
ASSUMPTION: Fails (a) partly, because walks are chosen in non-random situations, which confounds naive retrospective comparisons.
UNKNOWN: league_wide_intentional_walk_frequency_trend_since_rule_change

IDEA: Cross-cutting test design that applies to all ideas above. Use decision-point-level retrospective evaluation, with propensity or situational matching where choices are confounded, and report break-even margins rather than claimed wins.
ASSUMPTION: Public tracking and play-by-play data are lawfully accessible and sufficiently complete for each decision type; this requires verification per source.
ASSUMPTION: A club-level advantage requires that Cubs practice actually differs from the model break-even; no public evidence was supplied either way.
UNKNOWN: current_chicago_cubs_practice_for_each_decision_type
UNKNOWN: supplied_evidence_none

text:
IDEA: Problem: infield depth and lateral alignment within the current shift restrictions. Owner: the defensive coordinator and advance staff. Decision: the pre-pitch infield placement for each plate appearance, made thousands of times per team-season. Cases: every ball in play league-wide with tracked fielder starting positions, for each season since the restrictions began. Observable outcome: batted-ball result (out, hit, extra bases) given launch characteristics and starting positions. Baseline: the default alignment by batter handedness and pull tendency. Intervention: a per-batter, per-pitcher-type alignment recommender, checked retrospectively against the default on held-out seasons.
ASSUMPTION: Public tracking data records fielder starting positions precisely enough and for enough of each season to separate alignment effects from batted-ball quality.
ASSUMPTION: Rule constraints leave enough room for alignment choices that the gap between a tuned and a default alignment is meaningful over a season. This could fail (c) if most clubs already use near-optimal legal alignments.
ASSUMPTION: Batters do not change their spray behavior quickly in response to alignment. If they do, the retrospective test overstates the gain.
UNKNOWN: public_fielder_start_position_coverage_by_season
UNKNOWN: cubs_current_infield_alignment_policy
IDEA: Problem: timing of level-to-level minor-league promotions (for example High-A to Double-A), excluding minor-league-to-MLB call-ups, which were already explored. Owner: the farm director. Decision: whether to promote a prospect now or hold them, made many times per organization each season. Cases: every intra-minor-league promotion league-wide, reconstructable from public transaction logs and level-by-level stat lines. Observable outcome: performance at the next level over a fixed window, plus later public outcomes such as reaching MLB or stalling. Baseline: promote after a fixed playing-time threshold combined with an age-for-level rule. Intervention: a model using public underlying indicators (strikeout and walk rates, contact quality where available) to flag early-promote and hold candidates.
ASSUMPTION: Promotion timing has a causal effect on development rather than just reflecting talent. Promoted players are selected, so a naive comparison will be confounded. This fails (a)'s usefulness unless a credible comparison design exists.
ASSUMPTION: Public minor-league tracking data is consistent enough across levels and seasons to serve as pre-decision information. This is a risk to (d).
ASSUMPTION: The value at stake accumulates across many prospects to something meaningful for one club. This is plausible for (c), but outcomes lag by years.
UNKNOWN: public_minor_league_transaction_completeness
UNKNOWN: public_minor_league_statcast_coverage_by_level_and_season
IDEA: Problem: year-over-year workload progression for minor-league pitchers. Owner: the pitching coordinator and medical staff. Decision: each pitcher's innings or pitch-count ceiling and in-season pacing, set for every pitcher in an organization each year. Cases: thousands of pitcher-seasons league-wide with public innings, appearance and pitch-count logs. Observable outcome: publicly reported injured-list placements and next-season availability. Baseline: a fixed percentage increase over the prior season's innings. Intervention: a pacing rule that also uses public signals such as velocity trends, pitches per inning, and short-rest appearances.
ASSUMPTION: Public injured-list records for minor-league pitchers capture injuries reliably. Underreporting would break (b).
ASSUMPTION: Workload is a meaningful driver of injury compared with unobserved biomechanics. If not, the intervention has a low ceiling, similar to the R001 result.
ASSUMPTION: Velocity data is publicly available at enough minor-league levels to be a pre-decision input.
UNKNOWN: minor_league_il_reporting_completeness
UNKNOWN: public_minor_league_pitch_count_availability
IDEA: Problem: individualized hitter approach plans (swing or take by count and pitch zone) against a specific opposing starter. Owner: the hitting coaches. Decision: the pre-game plan for each hitter in each game, made daily. Cases: every plate appearance league-wide, with public pitch-level data on swing decisions. Observable outcome: swing-decision quality and run value per plate appearance against that pitcher type. Baseline: a uniform team approach adjusted only for pitcher handedness. Intervention: plans that match each hitter's demonstrated swing-decision weaknesses to the opposing pitcher's location and count tendencies.
ASSUMPTION: The retrospective test cannot observe what plan a hitter was given. Only the mismatch between hitter tendencies and pitcher tendencies can be measured, so the test checks for opportunity rather than the effect of the intervention. This is a failure on (b) for the intervention itself.
ASSUMPTION: Hitters can execute plan changes within a game without losing performance elsewhere.
ASSUMPTION: Opposing pitchers do not adapt within the series. This overlaps with the explored pitch-sequence family and needs separation.
UNKNOWN: cubs_existing_hitter_plan_process
IDEA: Problem: converting minor-league players to new positions (for example shortstop to second base or center field, or position player to pitcher). Owner: the player development director. Decision: whether and when to convert, made a moderate number of times per organization each year. Cases: conversions league-wide are identifiable from public appearance-by-position logs, but they number far fewer than promotions. Observable outcome: defensive metrics at the new position where public, plus offensive trajectory and progression to MLB. Baseline: convert when a player's age-for-level and error or range proxies fall below a threshold. Intervention: a model predicting the defensive value gain from a move using public batted-ball and sprint data.
ASSUMPTION: Enough conversions happen league-wide each season for statistical power. This is likely marginal on (a), and conversions to pitcher may be too rare.
ASSUMPTION: Public minor-league defensive metrics exist and are reliable. If not, (b) fails.
UNKNOWN: count_of_public_identifiable_position_conversions_per_season
IDEA: Problem: choosing which player to take within a draft round, as distinct from the explored bonus-pool allocation. Owner: the scouting director. Decision: hundreds of picks league-wide each year, including about one per round for each club. Cases: many draft classes of public pick lists linked to public pro outcomes. Observable outcome: progress through the minors and MLB value, observed only after many years. Baseline: consensus public prospect rankings. Intervention: a model reweighting public amateur performance data against the consensus.
ASSUMPTION: This is included as a challenge case. It meets (a) and (d) partly, but fails timeliness on (b) because outcomes lag by five or more years. Public amateur data may also be thin compared with private scouting, which weakens (d).
ASSUMPTION: Public consensus rankings already incorporate most public information, which would leave little room above the baseline.
UNKNOWN: historical_public_consensus_ranking_archives_availability
UNKNOWN: public_amateur_tracking_data_coverage
IDEA: Problem: scheduling rest days for everyday position players during the season. This is distinct from the explored travel planning family because the trigger is player performance and fatigue signals rather than travel. Owner: the manager and performance staff. Decision: which regular sits on which day, made many times per team-season. Cases: every regular's games-played sequence league-wide is public. Observable outcome: performance and sprint-speed trends after rest compared with continued play, plus injured-list placements. Baseline: rest each regular on a fixed cadence or on day games after night games. Intervention: rest triggered by public signals such as sprint-speed decline, bat-speed decline, and the opposing starter's handedness.

IDEA: Problem: third-base-coach send/hold choices on runners trying to score from second on a single or from first on a double. Owner: third-base coach, with advance and analytics staff preparing per-opponent cards. Decision: send or hold, made many times per season. Historical cases: league-wide, every such play in tracked MLB games across multiple seasons. Observable outcome: runner safe, out, or held, plus the later run expectancy of the resulting base-out state. Simple baseline: the coach's current tendency, or a rule based on runner speed tier and outfielder depth. Intervention: a pregame card giving send thresholds by opposing outfielder arm, transfer time, depth, runner sprint speed, outs and score state.
ASSUMPTION: Public tracking data records outfielder fielding position, throw speed and runner speed precisely enough to rebuild the conditions at the moment of decision.
ASSUMPTION: Held runners' counterfactual outcomes can be estimated without bias, even though holds are only observed when the coach chose to hold, so selection bias is severe.
ASSUMPTION: A coach can use a simple per-opponent card in a split-second decision. If not, criterion (d) fails at execution even if the analysis succeeds.
ASSUMPTION: The total value over a season is meaningful rather than a few runs. This must be measured, not assumed, and criterion (c) may fail.

UNKNOWN: magnitude_of_league_wide_send_hold_inefficiency

IDEA: Problem: outfielder throw-target choices, such as throwing home versus hitting the cutoff to hold the trailing runner. Owner: outfield coach and defensive coordinator. Decision: throw target on each runner-advance play, made many times per season. Historical cases: league-wide, all outfield hits with runners on in tracked games. Observable outcome: lead runner out or safe, trailing runner advanced or not, and run expectancy after the play. Simple baseline: always throw to the lead runner's base, or coach discretion. Intervention: a pregame matrix of throw targets by fielder arm, runner speeds and base-out state.
ASSUMPTION: Throw target is identifiable in public data. It may need video labeling, which raises cost and threatens criterion (b).
ASSUMPTION: Fielders can follow a prepared matrix under game conditions.
ASSUMPTION: This is distinct from positioning work, because it concerns the decision after the catch rather than alignment.

IDEA: Problem: runner tag-up and advance decisions on fly balls and balls in the dirt. Owner: baserunning coordinator and first- and third-base coaches. Decision: go or stay, made many times per season. Historical cases: league-wide, every fly ball with a runner on third or second and fewer than two outs, plus pitches in the dirt with runners on. Observable outcome: advance, out, or stay, and the resulting run expectancy. Simple baseline: a fixed rule such as "tag on any medium-depth fly," or current club tendencies. Intervention: opponent-specific go thresholds using catcher block and transfer metrics, outfielder arm and catch-point depth, and runner speed.
ASSUMPTION: Catcher blocking and outfielder throwing metrics are stable enough within a season to justify thresholds specific to each opponent.

Observable outcome: call overturned or confirmed, and loss of challenge capacity. Simple baseline: challenge whenever the replay room signals "likely," or challenge late-game close plays only. ASSUMPTION: Marginal roster spots carry enough value to satisfy criterion (c). This may fail if their replacement-level differences are tiny.

IDEA: Lineup batting-order construction (owner: manager with analytics staff; decision: daily order of the nine starters, about 162 times per club per season). Historical cases: every lineup card league-wide, publicly recorded per game in play-by-play archives. Observable outcome: plate appearances by lineup slot and runs scored. Simple baseline: a fixed template such as best on-base hitters at the top and the power hitter in a middle slot. Intervention: a run-expectancy simulator that suggests order swaps using projected platoon matchups and probable opposing relievers, plus a record of when the manager overrode it.
ASSUMPTION: Public analyses commonly treat batting-order effects as small per game; season-level value may fail criterion (c) even if criterion (a) is strongly satisfied.
ASSUMPTION: The counterfactual of runs under a different order cannot be observed, so retrospective tests depend on simulation rather than on outcome comparison; this weakens criterion (b).
ASSUMPTION: Order can affect player comfort or preparation in ways that public data does not capture.

UNKNOWN: public_estimate_of_order_effect_size_for_validation

IDEA: Manager replay challenge selection (owner: manager and replay-review staff; decision: whether to challenge a close call, many opportunities per club-season). Historical cases: every challenge league-wide since expanded replay, with outcomes in public records; declined opportunities are only partly observable. Observable outcome: call overturned, confirmed, or stands, and the change in run or win expectancy. Simple baseline: challenge when the replay coordinator's confidence feels high, saving challenges for late innings. Intervention: a calibration ledger of coordinator confidence versus result, plus a leverage-weighted threshold that changes by inning and by challenges remaining.
ASSUMPTION: Unchallenged close plays are not systematically logged in public data, so the denominator of opportunities is missing; this partially fails criterion (a) for the "should have challenged" side.
ASSUMPTION: Coordinator confidence would have to be recorded prospectively by the club; public data cannot reconstruct it.
ASSUMPTION: Value per overturned call may be modest; the season total for criterion (c) needs verification.
UNKNOWN: public_dataset_of_unchallenged_close_plays
UNKNOWN: overturn_rate_by_play_type_public_source

IDEA: Position-player pitching and mop-up allocation (owner: manager and pitching coach; decision: who pitches in low-leverage blowout innings, many times per club-season). Historical cases: every low-leverage relief inning league-wide, with leverage measurable from public play-by-play. Observable outcome: runs allowed in the blowout, plus the workload and next-days availability of affected relievers. Simple baseline: use the last reliever on the depth chart, or a position player past a fixed run-differential threshold. Intervention: a rule that weighs comeback probability against the expected cost of reliever fatigue over the following series.
ASSUMPTION: The downstream fatigue cost is inferred rather than observed; outcome attribution for criterion (b) is weak.
ASSUMPTION: Eligibility rules for position-player pitching have changed over time, which shrinks the comparable pool for criterion (a).
ASSUMPTION: Overlap with the explored "opposing bullpen availability" family is partial; this idea concerns the club's own bullpen.
UNKNOWN: current_position_player_pitching_eligibility_rule
UNKNOWN: measurable_link_between_mop_up_usage_and_next_day_performance

IDEA: Affiliate level-to-level promotion timing within the minor leagues (owner: farm director; decision: when to promote a prospect from one minor-league level to the next, dozens of moves per organization-season). Historical cases: thousands of public level changes league-wide in MiLB transaction and stat records. Observable outcome: performance and age-relative-to-level at the new level, and eventual MLB arrival. Simple baseline: promote after a fixed time-at-level or a statistical threshold. Intervention: a public-data hazard model of how hitters and pitchers struggle or adjust after promotion, used to flag prospects who are likely ready early or too late.
ASSUMPTION: Promotion choices are confounded by private scouting, injury, and roster need, so a retrospective comparison is selection-biased; criterion (b) is observable but not causal.
ASSUMPTION: This differs from the explored "call-up translation" family because it concerns minor-to-minor moves; it could still be judged duplicative.
ASSUMPTION: Value for criterion (c) shows up over years rather than within one season.
UNKNOWN: completeness_of_public_minor_league_transaction_history
UNKNOWN: whether_public_minor_league_pitch_tracking_covers_all_levels_consistently

IDEA: Amateur draft pick selection in middle and late rounds (owner: scouting director; decision: choice at each pick, many picks per club per year). Historical cases: every pick league-wide each year, with public draft records and later public career stats. Observable outcome: signing status, minor-league progression, and MLB appearances, observable after a long lag. Simple baseline: follow a consensus public prospect ranking, or use college performance thresholds. Intervention: a model that measures how far the club deviates from public consensus and which deviation types later paid off league-wide.
ASSUMPTION: Outcome lag of several years fails the timeliness side of criterion (b) for any near-term test.
ASSUMPTION: Signability and bonus negotiation are counterparty-driven and overlap the explored bonus-pool family.
ASSUMPTION: Archived public consensus rankings from before each draft may be incomplete for later rounds; this threatens criterion (d).
UNKNOWN: archived_pre_draft_public_rankings_depth
UNKNOWN: public_amateur_performance_data_coverage

IDEA: Late-inning defensive replacement decisions (owner: manager and bench coach; decision: whether to substitute a better fielder when protecting a lead, many times per club-season). Historical cases: every late-game defensive substitution, plus every non-substitution, reconstructable from public play-by-play and lineup changes. Observable outcome: balls in play to the replaced position and runs allowed in the remaining innings. Simple baseline: always replace a designated weak fielder when leading in the late innings. Intervention: a leverage-aware rule that includes the cost of losing the original bat if the game goes to extra innings.
ASSUMPTION: Few balls reach any one position per inning, so the per-decision signal is noisy; criterion (a) may hold while effective statistical power stays low.
ASSUMPTION: Overlap with the explored "bench" families needs checking.
UNKNOWN: public_fielding_run_value_granularity_by_inning
UNKNOWN: extra_inning_frequency_needed_for_cost_term

UNKNOWN: club_simple_rule_for_each_decision
UNKNOWN: minimum_detectable_effect_per_family
